title: Only 1 Dollar in 10 Is Cash. How Banks Create Money Out of Thin Air
description:
Only about 1 dollar in 10 in America is physical cash: $2.5 trillion of currency out of $23.4 trillion in M2 (September 2026). Most of the rest was created by banks when they made loans. A loan doesn't lend out someone else's savings: it creates a brand-new deposit, and paying the loan back destroys that money. The Bank of England explained this in 2014.

We follow a $300,000 mortgage through a bank's books, show where cash fits in, why the US reserve requirement has been 0% since March 2020, what really limits banks (borrowers, capital, interest rates and confidence), what happened at Silicon Valley Bank, and how the 2020 money flood (M2 up about 40%, the Fed's balance sheet from $4.2 trillion to almost $9 trillion) came before 9% inflation.

Sources: Bank of England, "Money creation in the modern economy", Quarterly Bulletin 2014 Q1 (McLeay, Radia and Thomas). Federal Reserve: reserve requirement ratios set to 0% effective March 26, 2020; "Review of the Federal Reserve's Supervision and Regulation of Silicon Valley Bank" (April 2023): $42 billion withdrawn on March 9, 2023. FDIC: deposit insurance up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each account ownership category. FRED (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis): M2SL, WCURCIR (currency in circulation), WALCL (Fed total assets), TOTRESNS (reserves), DPSACBW027SBOG (commercial bank deposits), TOTLL (loans and leases), CPIAUCSL (CPI, 12-month change), MORTGAGE30US (Freddie Mac 30-year fixed, Oct 22, 2026: 7.32%), SNDR (FDIC national savings rate, Oct 2026: 0.38%). Mortgage example: $300,000, 30 years, fixed 7.32%, about $2,061 a month, about $742,000 paid in total; taxes and insurance not included.
